claims.text: At low SRO volume fraction, isolated SRO clusters reduce thermal conductivity by scattering phonons.
Above a critical SRO percolation threshold, thermal conductivity increases.
Percolated SRO suppresses anharmonic phonon-phonon scattering.
Coherent, low-disorder SRO pathways facilitate ballistic phonon transport.
The random-solid-solution state of the bcc refractory HEA has high lattice distortion.
The random-solid-solution state exhibits significant anharmonic phonon scattering.
Thermo-mechanical processing such as intermediate-temperature annealing or controlled quenching can nucleate and grow SRO clusters.
Continued SRO growth can produce a connected, percolating network of ordered regions in a disordered matrix.
The target alloy remains single-phase bcc at operating temperatures above 1000 K.
Operating near but below the order-disorder transition temperature preserves stable SRO.
A percolating network of chemically ordered SRO clusters provides a continuous pathway with reduced lattice distortion.
Isolated SRO clusters primarily behave as phonon-scattering centers.
SRO percolation reduces the density of random-solute scattering events.
Coherent ordered domains lower the effective Grüneisen parameter.
Thermal conductivity has a minimum at low SRO fraction and rises sharply at the SRO percolation threshold.
At high SRO connectivity, thermal conductivity may exceed that of the random solid solution.
Standard serial or parallel mixing models and simple scattering theories predict a monotonic conductivity decrease as SRO increases.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to SRO that does not transform into a distinct second phase such as L21 or D03.
Whether percolated SRO raises conductivity depends on the phonon mean free path relative to SRO cluster size.
A simulation potential must accurately represent the energy cost of diffuse antiphase boundaries to predict SRO-network stability.
